title: Nothing Gets Out Unescaped: A Run Through MarkupSafe
premise: A web page wants to show a comment somebody posted: `<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>`. Printed as-is into HTML, that string stops being text and starts being code — it is a cross-site scripting payload. MarkupSafe exists to make the difference between "text" and "markup" a property of the value itself, carried in its type, so that a template can mix trusted and untrusted pieces and the untrusted ones can only ever arrive as inert characters. This story follows that one untrusted comment from the moment it is handed to `escape()` until it comes back out of a rendered fragment as plain text again, and notes at each step exactly what is guaranteed, what is merely trusted, and who is responsible for which.

chapters.title: The Trust Boundary, and the Unguarded Door Beside It
chapters.data_in: s = '<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>' — a plain str of unknown provenance
chapters.data_out: Markup('<script>alert(document.cookie);</script>'), and the same value again after a second trip through escape()
facts: `escape` tests `type(s) is str`, not `isinstance`, so the fast path is taken only by exact `str`; the comment qualifies and skips the `__html__` check entirely (__init__.py:39-40).
The comment on lines 37-38 says `type(s)` is deliberate: a proxy object can lie about `__class__`, so `isinstance` would be a trust hole; `tests/test_escape.py::test_proxy` pins this.

`_escape_inner` replaces exactly five characters \u2014 `&`, `>`, `<`, `'`, `"` \u2014 and nothing else (_native.py:1-8). Backtick, `=`, and whitespace are untouched; safety of attribute values therefore assumes the attribute is quoted.
`_native` replaces `&` first, before the four replacements that introduce `&`; reversing that order would double-escape every entity.

At import time the C version from `_speedups` is preferred and the pure-Python `_native` is the fallback (__init__.py:7-10). The C code escapes the same five characters for 1-, 2- and 4-byte strings and returns the *same object* when nothing needs escaping (_speedups.c:84-87).
`Markup.__new__` performs no escaping whatsoever. It wraps whatever text it is given and declares it safe (__init__.py:122-131); before wrapping it calls `object.__html__()` if that attribute exists.
`__new__` accepts `encoding`/`errors` and only forwards them to `str.__new__` when `encoding is not None` \u2014 the bytes-decoding road, not taken here.

`__repr__` wraps `str.__repr__` in the class name, so a `Markup` is visually distinguishable from a `str` in logs and REPLs (__init__.py:167-168). `Markup` sets `__slots__ = ()`: the safety flag is the type, nothing more.

Re-escaping the result takes a different branch: `Markup` is a `str` subclass, so `type(s) is str` is False and `hasattr(s, "__html__")` wins; `Markup.__html__` returns `self` (__init__.py:133-134), so escaping is idempotent and the five replacements never run twice.

The trace shows `__html__` called twice on that round trip \u2014 once by `escape`, once again inside `Markup.__new__`, which re-checks for it. Harmless for `Markup`, but a user-defined `__html__` with side effects or cost is invoked twice per `escape` call.

Road not taken: a `str` subclass *without* `__html__` (e.g. `tests/test_escape.py::ReferenceStr`) falls to the third branch, `Markup(_escape_inner(str(s)))`. That branch is also why `escape(None)` yields `Markup('None')`, and why `escape_silent` exists (__init__.py:48-61).

open_questions.question: If `Markup()` will bless any string at all, and `__html__` output is taken on faith, what stops untrusted text from being wrapped \u2014 and who is accountable when it is?
Escaping a `Markup` returns a `Markup` \u2014 but what if an application subclasses `Markup`? Does the subclass survive a round trip through `escape`?

chapters.title: An Object That Writes Its Own HTML, and a Template That Escapes Its Arguments
chapters.data_in:
a User instance with id=3 and name='Alice "The Great"'; then '

User: {user:link} said: {comment}

' wrapped as Markup
chapters.data_out: repr 'Markup(\'Alice ...lt;b>Great</b>"\')'; then control inside User.__html_format__, holding Markup('{}')
facts: `escape(user)` takes the `hasattr(s, "__html__")` branch: the object's own markup is wrapped in `Markup` and never escaped, so MarkupSafe trusts it verbatim. This `User` is careful \u2014 it builds its span via `Markup(...).format(name)` \u2014 but the library cannot check that an arbitrary `__html__` did so; `docs/html.rst:31-43` states this responsibility explicitly.
Exceptions raised inside `__html__` propagate out of `escape` rather than being swallowed; this was a historical segfault in the C path and is pinned by `tests/test_exception_custom_html.py`.
The *template* text is trusted because it is a `Markup`; only the substituted values get escaped. Calling `.format()` on an untrusted template string would not be protected by anything here.

`Markup.format` builds a fresh `EscapeFormatter(self.escape)` per call and hands off to `string.Formatter.vformat` (__init__.py:313-315) \u2014 standard-library parsing, custom field rendering. Because the escape callable is the bound classmethod of the actual class, subclasses format into their own type. `format_map` is the same machinery with an empty args tuple.

Road not taken: the `%` operator (`__mod__`, __init__.py:154-165) wraps each argument in `_MarkupEscapeHelper`, which escapes lazily in `__str__`/`__repr__` and passes `__int__`/`__float__` through unescaped \u2014 a different path to the same guarantee, exercised by `tests/test_markupsafe.py::test_string_interpolation`.

`format_field` dispatches in a fixed order: `__html_format__` first, then `__html__`, then Python's default `super().format_field` (__init__.py:340-353). Because `__html_format__` wins, `User` receives the raw spec string `'link'` and decides what it means; MarkupSafe imposes no spec grammar.

Road not taken: an object with `__html__` but no `__html_format__` *and* a non-empty spec raises `ValueError` naming the type (__init__.py:343-348), so specs are never silently dropped. `Markup.__html_format__` likewise raises for any non-empty spec (__init__.py:325-329) \u2014 `{:>10}` on a `Markup` is an error, not a pad.
In the default branch the spec is coerced with `str(format_spec)` before delegating, so a `Markup` spec does not invoke the wrong `__format__` callbacks.
The whole dispatch is `hasattr`-based duck typing: any object claiming these method names is believed.
`EscapeFormatter` declares `__slots__` but subclasses `string.Formatter`, which does not \u2014 so the slots save nothing; cosmetic, not a risk.

open_questions.question: `format_field` ends with `str(self.escape(rv))`, handing back a bare `str` and losing the safe type. Does the final result still come out as `Markup`, or has the guarantee leaked away mid-render?

answers.answer: Nothing in the library stops it: both `Markup(text)` and a loose `__html__` implementation bless text unchecked. The guarantee is one-directional \u2014 `escape()` output is safe; `Markup()` / `__html__` input is the application author's responsibility, and the docs say so.

chapters.title: The Innermost Escape: the user's name
chapters.data_out: Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"'), then the completed Markup('…')
facts: The name is a plain `str` with no `__html__`, so it reaches the third branch: `super().format_field(value, str(''))` and then `str(self.escape(rv))` (__init__.py:350-354).
Escaping converts `"` to `"` and ``/`` to `<b>`/`</b>`: the double quote matters because the name lands next to quoted attribute values elsewhere in the page.
`format_field` returns a plain `str`, not a `Markup` \u2014 the type is stripped deliberately, because `string.Formatter.vformat` concatenates fields with plain string operations.
Escaping happens on the *rendered* field, so numbers, dates and anything else produced by Python's default format machinery are escaped too (`tests/test_markupsafe.py::test_formatting_with_objects`).

The inner `Markup('{}').format(...)` runs the same path twice more (trace line 44, elided): once for `self.id`, an int that escapes to itself, and once for the already-safe span, which takes the `__html__` branch and is inserted verbatim.
`Markup.format` wraps the joined result with `self.__class__(...)`, which is where the inner fragment regains its safe type before being handed back to the outer render.

open_questions.question: `__html_format__` returned a `Markup` rather than a plain string. When that value is substituted into the outer template, does it get escaped a second time \u2014 turning the anchor tag into visible text?

chapters.title: Markup.escape and the Reassembled Page
chapters.data_in: s = Markup('Alice "The <b>Great</b>"'), plus the remaining {comment} field
facts: `Markup.escape` is a classmethod that calls the module-level `escape` and then, only if `rv.__class__ is not cls`, re-wraps the result in `cls` (__init__.py:235-240) \u2014 so a `Markup` subclass gets its own type back.

The value returned by `User.__html_format__` is already a `Markup`, so the run takes the `__html__` path and the markup survives verbatim: the `<a>` and `<span>` tags are not escaped while the name inside them stays escaped.
The common case (`rv.__class__ is cls`) returns the object `escape` built rather than constructing another \u2014 one allocation saved on the hot path.
The `{comment}` field (trace line 56, the same `format_field` path told once already) also takes the `__html__` branch, so the pre-escaped comment is inserted without a second round of escaping.

`vformat` joins the trusted literal template text with the escaped field strings into one plain `str`; `Markup.format` then wraps that whole string with `self.__class__(...)` (__init__.py:315) \u2014 that final wrap is where the type-level guarantee is restored.
The resulting fragment contains `<script>` and never `<script>` \u2014 the scenario's `assert "<script>" not in page` holds by construction, not by inspection.

Failure mode worth knowing: a malformed field in the template raises from `string.Formatter`, and a missing `%`-style argument raises `TypeError` in the `__mod__` path (`tests/test_markupsafe.py::test_missing_interpol`) \u2014 formatting errors surface loudly rather than producing partial output.

answers.answer: Yes: `Markup.escape` compares `rv.__class__` with `cls` and re-wraps when they differ, so escaping, formatting, joining and concatenation on a `Markup` subclass all return that subclass.

The bare strings are only an internal convenience: `vformat` concatenates them and `Markup.format` wraps the whole joined result in `self.__class__`, so the value that leaves the call is a `Markup` again.
No \u2014 `Markup.escape` routes it through `escape`, which sees `__html__` and returns the text unchanged. Safe fragments nest inside safe fragments without ever being escaped twice.

chapters.title: Concatenation: the operand gets escaped, both ways
facts: `Markup.__add__` escapes its right operand with `self.escape(value)` and wraps the concatenation in `self.__class__` (__init__.py:136-140) \u2014 so `safe + untrusted` is safe, which is the most common real-world use after `escape` itself.
The second `+` has a `Markup` on the right; it goes through the same `Markup.escape` call and comes back unchanged, so safe + safe does not double-escape.

`__add__` guards with `isinstance(value, str) or hasattr(value, "__html__")` and returns `NotImplemented` otherwise; Python then raises `TypeError`. Adding an int to a `Markup` fails loudly rather than stringifying it.
`__radd__` mirrors this for `plain + markup`, escaping the left operand first (__init__.py:142-146), so direction does not matter.

The same wrap-and-escape pattern covers the rest of the `str` API: `join` escapes every element, `replace` escapes only its `new` argument, and `ljust`/`rjust`/`center` escape the fill character, while `strip`, `lstrip`, `rstrip`, `removeprefix`/`removesuffix` and `partition` deliberately do *not* escape their arguments (CHANGES.rst 3.0.0) because they are search operations, not insertion.

`split`, `rsplit`, `splitlines`, `partition` and `__getitem__` return `Markup` pieces \u2014 slicing safe markup can still split an entity in half, producing well-typed but malformed output. A real sharp edge, accepted by design.

open_questions.question: Everything so far has only added safety. Is there any operation here that hands back text that is *not* safe \u2014 and would the type still say so?

chapters.title: striptags: the exit back to plain text, and what the fragment guarantees
chapters.data_out: 'User: Alice "The Great" said: ' — a plain str with live script text in it; and a final Markup rebuilt from a developer-written literal
inputs: the expected fragment as a literal str
facts: `striptags` strips comments first, in their own loop, then tags; the comment at __init__.py:208-210 explains why \u2014 a comment containing a `<em>` would otherwise end early and leak the rest of the comment into the output.

Both loops use plain `find` rather than regular expressions; this was changed in 2.1.4 to avoid a catastrophic-backtracking performance issue (CHANGES.rst), so input size cannot blow up the runtime. An unterminated `<!--` or `<` makes the loop `break`, leaving the remainder in place \u2014 stripping is best-effort, not a sanitizer.

The last step is `self.__class__(value).unescape()`, and `unescape` returns `str(self)` passed through `html.unescape` \u2014 the return type is `str`, *not* `Markup`. The escaped `<script>` becomes a live `<script>` again; whoever calls it owns the result.

`striptags` and `unescape` are the documented way out of safety, and the `-> str` annotation is the only warning the type system gives. In review, any path where their output flows back into a template without a fresh `escape` \u2014 or any `Markup(...)` wrapped around a non-literal \u2014 is the thing to flag.
The closing `Markup(...)` on the expected fragment is the same unguarded constructor from chapter 1, used here on a developer-written literal: the legitimate use, text the author controls.

The guarantee, stated plainly: anything that passes through `escape` (directly, or via `format`, `%`, `+`, `join`, `replace`, `ljust`/`rjust`/`center`) has `& > < ' "` replaced and is typed `Markup`; a `Markup` fed back through any of those paths is not escaped again.

The non-guarantees: `Markup(text)` and user-defined `__html__`/`__html_format__` are trusted without checks; only five characters are escaped, so unquoted HTML attributes, `javascript:` URLs, inline `<script>`/`<style>` contexts and JS/CSS string contexts are out of scope; `striptags`/`unescape` return unsafe `str`; slicing can cut an entity in half; `__html__` may be called twice per `escape`.

Convenience helpers at the edge: `escape_silent(None)` yields `Markup('')` where `escape(None)` would yield `Markup('None')` (__init__.py:48-61), and `soft_str` stringifies without destroying an existing `Markup` (__init__.py:64-81) \u2014 the function to reach for instead of `str()` when passing markup around.
The C and pure-Python implementations are interchangeable and chosen at import; `tests/conftest.py` runs the whole suite against both, so a missing C extension changes speed, not behaviour.

answers.answer: Yes \u2014 `striptags` and `unescape` deliberately undo escaping and are annotated to return plain `str`, so the value loses both its entities and its safe type at the same moment.
